title: What survives a stop, pause or sleep
standfirst: Seven words — stop, pause, sleep, suspend, standby, hibernate, archive — describe four behaviours. The only question that matters is what is still running when the machine comes back.

concept.heading: Four behaviours behind seven words
paragraphs: Every provider in this set offers some way to make a machine cheaper while you are not using it. They fall into four behaviours. Disk only: the machine is destroyed and its disk is kept, so files survive and processes do not. Disk and memory: RAM is saved, so the agent's process tree can resume mid-task. Warm memory: the machine is frozen in the host's RAM, which resumes fastest and usually keeps billing for memory. Delete: the disk goes too.

The vocabulary is not standardised. InstaBox calls memory-preserving freeze “pause” and powers off with “stop”. Agent 37 has both, under the names `sleep` and `stop`. boxd has three parked states — standby, hibernate, stop — plus a separate destroy. Lizard's `stop` deletes the disk. Boat's API calls a stopped sandbox “archived”, and its homepage still says “pause billing” even though the docs state there is no pause.

concept.heading: Best-effort is not a guarantee
paragraphs: Even where memory is meant to survive, it often does not. Sandboxer restores memory only if a machine of the same CPU type is free within two minutes, and reports `memoryRestored: false` when it cold-boots instead. InstaBox reports `processesPreserved: false` on the same kind of fallback. Agent 37 says memory “usually survives a wake, but it is not guaranteed”, and a host move forces a fresh boot.
The practical rule: treat anything that must outlive a pause as a file. Memory-preserving resume is a convenience for short interruptions, not a storage strategy.

concept.heading: What a resume quietly resets
paragraphs: A cold resume is not just “processes stopped”. Boat's resume gives the sandbox a new IP, so anything that cached its own address is stale. Lizard's pause closes open network connections, so a long-lived WebSocket has to reconnect. boxd's clocks freeze while suspended, so cron and systemd timers miss their slots. InstaBox's resume can silently boot fresh while the API still says the machine is running.

comparisonIntro: Can the provider park a machine without losing the agent's running state, and what exactly survives?

rows.note: `sleep` keeps memory and processes as a checkpoint and bills disk only; `stop` keeps the disk and loses memory. A wake that has to rebuild boots fresh, and stopping a sleeper discards its checkpoint.

source.quote: Sleep and stop both release CPU and memory and bill disk alone. A sleeping instance keeps its memory and wakes on the next request; a stopped one loses its memory and stays down until `start`.

rows.note: A stop writes memory and device state to disk, so a resume can restore running processes — but only on a machine of the same CPU type within two minutes; otherwise it cold-boots. A resize resume is always a cold boot.

source.quote: Memory is restored on a machine with the same CPU type as the one the sandbox stopped on.

rows.note: Four distinct states: standby keeps RAM frozen (and bills it), hibernate writes memory to disk with an ~85 ms wake, stop keeps the disk only, destroy removes everything.

source.quote: They freeze the VMM process and keep memory, running processes, and open sockets intact.

rows.note: `pause` keeps memory and running programs and resumes in about a second; `stop` loses them, and a paused machine cannot be stopped at all. A resume can cold-boot and report `processesPreserved: false`.

source.quote: Pauses a running machine, keeping its memory and running programs.

rows.note: `pause` keeps the whole disk, memory and processes; `pause({fast: true})` keeps files only and resumes like a restart; `stop` or expiry deletes the sandbox's disk, leaving only `/workspace` and snapshots.

source.quote: A stop (kill or expiration) deletes the sandbox's disk: only files on an attached Persistent Volume at `/workspace` and the snapshots you took remain.

rows.note: `pause` freezes the VM with memory and programs intact; `stop` keeps files and drops memory. Both keep billing storage, and only delete ends the charge.

source.quote: `wake`: it carries on where it was

rows.note: There is no pause. `stop` saves the disk, removes the machine, and loses memory and hand-started processes; `resume` boots a new machine from the same disk with a new IP.

source.quote: There is no pause. A stop removes the virtual machine and keeps a copy of the disk.

questions: When the machine comes back, is my agent's process still running, or does it start fresh?
Does the provider's word for “off” keep memory, keep only the disk, or delete the disk?
Is a memory-preserving resume guaranteed, or best-effort with a cold-boot fallback?
What is lost that I would not think of — open sockets, cron timers, the machine's IP?
Does a stop reset the OS, installed packages, or files outside the home folder?
Does a paused machine keep billing for memory, and how much?

picks.situation: Resume exactly where the agent was, mid-tool-call
picks.why: These three keep memory and processes across a pause, so a half-finished turn can continue. boxd's fork and snapshot go further and copy a running machine.

picks.situation: A cheap idle state that still keeps everything installed
picks.why: The disk survives and memory does not. Boat charges nothing while stopped and keeps the disk 14 days; Agent 37 charges cents per GB-month; Sandboxer charges nothing within its storage quota.

picks.situation: Undo a bad change without losing the last hour
picks.why: boxd has in-place checkpoints (up to 10 per machine) and Sandboxer takes a disk snapshot every ten minutes. Most providers only offer a snapshot you take yourself, which does not help with a change you did not anticipate.

picks.situation: A long CPU-bound job that must not be interrupted
picks.why: Both can be configured not to sleep, and boxd's idle timer watches the network rather than the CPU, so a compile looks idle. Set boxd's auto-hibernate to 0, or it will hibernate at hour four.

picks.situation: Files must survive weeks of not being used
picks.why: Agent 37 and InstaBox keep the disk until you delete, and Sandboxer keeps stopped disks free within its quota. Boat's disk expires after 14 days, and Lizard's stop deletes it.

gotchas: Boat's homepage still says “pause billing”; its docs say there is no pause.
InstaBox cannot stop a paused machine, so a script that always calls stop breaks after an idle pause.
Lizard's default lifetime is five minutes from the SDK and CLI, and expiry deletes files outside `/workspace`.
boxd's idle timer counts TCP/UDP traffic in either direction, not CPU use: a long local compile looks idle, while polling an API keeps the box awake.
boxd's standby keeps RAM frozen in the host and keeps billing for it; hibernate is the cheap parked state.
A memory-preserving resume is usually best-effort. Check for a `memoryRestored` or `processesPreserved` flag rather than assuming.
